oneLineAnswer: A prescription tablet for certain advanced lung cancers that blocks a growth signal driving the tumor.
whatItIs: Afatinib is a prescription cancer medicine, sold as Gilotrif and as generic tablets. It belongs to a group of drugs called kinase inhibitors. A kinase is an enzyme that tags other proteins and can switch growth signals on. Afatinib targets EGFR, HER2 and HER4, three kinases that sit on cell surfaces. Some lung cancers carry a changed, or mutated, EGFR gene that keeps those signals switched on. Metastatic means the cancer has spread beyond where it started. The tablets contain afatinib dimaleate, a salt form of the drug. PubChem lists the molecular formula of afatinib itself as C24H25ClFN5O3.
whatItDoes: Afatinib binds to EGFR, HER2 and HER4 and blocks the signals that drive tumor growth.
In controlled trials, it lengthened the time before the cancer grew again (LiverTox).
The US label approves it for two groups of people with advanced lung cancer.
One group has metastatic non-small cell lung cancer with certain EGFR mutations, treated first.
The other has squamous lung cancer that worsened after platinum-based chemotherapy.
howPeopleUseIt: It is a tablet you swallow, taken on a daily schedule set by your cancer team.
LiverTox describes treatment as continuing until the cancer progresses or side effects become intolerable.
The label describes pausing or reducing treatment when certain side effects appear.
People on afatinib have regular checkups, including blood tests for liver function (label).
Researchers are studying afatinib combined with other cancer drugs (ClinicalTrials.gov).
Those trials include cancers of the esophagus, bile ducts and other advanced solid tumors.

commonSideEffects: Diarrhea is the most common problem; the label reports it in 96% of patients in one trial.
A rash or acne-like rash is common, often on the face or upper body.
Mouth sores, dry skin, itching and nail-fold infections also happen often.
Loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting are common.
The label reports that side effects led to a lower dose for 57% of patients in one trial.
seriousSigns: Severe or long-lasting diarrhea can dehydrate you and harm your kidneys; some cases were fatal.
Blistering, peeling or spreading skin reactions need prompt medical attention (label).
Rare severe skin reactions include Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Lung inflammation, called interstitial lung disease, occurred in 1.6% of patients in trials.
The label reports fatal liver failure in 0.2% of patients.
A hole in the stomach or intestine, called gastrointestinal perforation, occurred in 0.2%.
Eye inflammation, called keratitis, occurred in 0.7% of patients.
The label tells patients to report new trouble breathing, cough or fever.
LiverTox links afatinib to hepatitis B virus becoming active again during treatment.
whoShouldAvoid: The label lists no contraindication, meaning no group is barred from the drug outright.
Pregnancy is a reason to avoid it: animal studies show harm to the developing fetus.
Breastfeeding is not advised during treatment or for two weeks after the last tablet.
Children are not an approved group; safety and effectiveness are not established.
People with severe kidney impairment have higher levels of the drug in the body (label).
LiverTox says hepatitis B should be checked before treatment, because the virus can reactivate.

interactions: P-gp is a pump protein that moves some drugs out of cells.
P-gp inhibitors raise afatinib levels. The label names ritonavir, cyclosporine, ketoconazole, itraconazole and erythromycin.
That label list continues with verapamil, quinidine, tacrolimus, nelfinavir, saquinavir and amiodarone.
P-gp inducers lower afatinib levels. The label names rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital and St. John's wort.
For both kinds of interaction, the label describes adjusting the afatinib dose.
pregnancyAndChildren: Afatinib can harm a developing fetus. Rabbit studies found embryo loss and, in mothers showing toxicity, late abortion. Rat studies found delayed bone formation and lower fetal weight. There are no human pregnancy data. The label advises contraception during treatment and for at least two weeks after the last dose. Breastfeeding is not advised during treatment and for two weeks after it ends, because afatinib passed into rat milk. In children, safety and effectiveness are not established. One trial treated 37 children aged 2 to under 17 who had solid tumors. Their drug levels resembled adult levels and no new safety signals appeared. Animal data suggest afatinib may reduce fertility in females and males, and reversibility is unknown.
whatWeDoNotKnow: No human data exist on afatinib in pregnancy; the fetal risk comes from animal studies and its mechanism.
Whether fertility changes reverse after treatment ends is unknown (label).
LiverTox says the timing and pattern of afatinib liver injury have not been published.
The label notes trial side-effect rates cannot be compared directly between medicines.
The main first-line trial enrolled too few people aged 65 and older to compare responses (label).
Most combination trials are still recruiting or of unknown status, so their results are pending.
No source found here reports how often hepatitis B reactivates on afatinib outside trial settings.

gaps: NCCIH has no afatinib page: https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/afatinib returned HTTP 404, so no NCCIH content appears here.
NCBI Bookshelf refused plain fetches of the LiverTox chapter with a browser and captcha check; the chapter was read in the in-app browser instead, and its seven quotes come from that page.
The NCI drug dictionary page returned only a navigation shell with no drug text, so NCI is not cited.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were excluded on purpose, because NLM states they are American Society of Health-System Pharmacists content. No MedlinePlus page is cited.

OpenFDA and DailyMed both carry FDA-authored label text, so they are separate publishers but not independent sources for label content. LiverTox, PubChem and ClinicalTrials.gov are independent of the label.
No dose amounts, schedules or personal plans are written here by design, so that is not a sourcing gap.
No human pregnancy or breastfeeding data were found in the fetched sources; both are described only from animal findings.
The ClinicalTrials.gov records were read as titles, statuses and phases only, so no results or outcome data from those trials are reported.
No source found here states how often hepatitis B reactivates during afatinib treatment in routine practice.
Side-effect rates come from trial populations, and the label warns those rates may not match ordinary practice.
summary: This record covers what afatinib is and how it blocks EGFR-family signaling, its two approved lung cancer uses, its common and serious risks, its P-gp interactions, and the questions the fetched sources leave open.
